extracted.intended_audience: general readers, academics, journalists and others interested in academic publishing and hoaxes
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article summarizing the Grievance Studies Affair: the planning, submission, publication outcomes, reactions, and critiques of a series of deliberately bogus academic papers submitted to journals. It covers ethical, methodological, and editorial issues raised by the stunt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed conclusions vs objective truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The trio described 'grievance studies' as areas 'in which only certain conclusions are allowed [...] and put social grievances ahead of objective truth'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by the hoaxers as a substantive critique of some fields; implies a rubric that good scholarship should not begin from a foregone conclusion but should respect evidentiary standards and openness to refutation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research ethics — no fabrication or deceptive submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and critics emphasised that 'the idea that individuals would submit fraudulent academic material violates many ethical and academic norms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting fabricated authors, data, or claims is cited as unethical and can violate publication contracts, trigger misconduct inquiries, and incur retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author identity verification / contractual obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender, Place & Culture suspected the pseudonymous author had 'breached their contract to "not [fabricate] or [misappropriate] anyone's identity, including [their] own"' and requested documentation confirming identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may require proof of identity and reserve contractual remedies for misrepresentation; author authenticity is a baseline requirement for publication ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-subjects approval / IRB compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Portland State University initiated an inquiry on grounds of 'conducting human subject–based research without approval' and considered a charge of fabricating data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research involving human subjects normally requires prior institutional approval; failing to obtain it constitutes a serious ethical and procedural violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design — need for control group and valid methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Some critics argued the project 'did not represent a scientific investigation, given that the project did not include a control group', and that without comparison it is impossible to draw broad conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To claim generalizable findings from a sting or experiment, include controls and transparent methodology; absence of these undermines evidentiary claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review limitations — peer review is not designed to detect fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics noted 'peer review is not designed to remove fraud or even absurd ideas', and that peer review has limits in policing fabricated or fraudulent material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate peer review with fraud detection; replication and post-publication scrutiny are needed for corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal impact factor correlates with editorial stringency
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis found 'journals with higher impact factors were more likely to reject papers submitted as part of the project.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impact factor was observed as a proxy for selectivity in this case; authors and critics may use journal metrics as one indicator of editorial rigor, though it is not definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of (alleged) empirical data increases acceptance chances
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers found 'the chances were better, if the manuscript was allegedly based on empirical data.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers presenting empirical claims (even fabricated) were more likely to be taken seriously by reviewers/editors; empirical appearance can influence acceptance but must be genuine and verifiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness to reviewer feedback as path to acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: The project authors, 'when ... closely followed the reviewers' advice, were able to learn relatively quickly what is needed for writing an acceptable article.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully addressing peer-review comments and revising manuscripts is a key factor in editorial acceptance; iterative revision is part of scholarly quality assurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary mimicry — blurred boundary between serious work and hoax
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers noted 'the boundary between a seriously written paper and a "hoax" gradually became blurred.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successfully imitating field-specific jargon, methods, and rhetorical styles can make low-quality or bogus work appear credible; reviewers rely on substantive checks beyond surface style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of target journals affects outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics observed 'It is unclear, on what grounds the project group decided what journals to target.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeting particular journals (by scope, selectivity, editorial practices) influences acceptance rates and the evidentiary value of any sting; transparent selection criteria are needed for defensible conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication safeguards — expressions of concern and retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: The article documents instances of 'Expression of Concern' and later retractions for some published hoax papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retractions, expressions of concern, and editorial notes are mechanisms journals use to correct the literature when fraud or serious problems are discovered; reliance on post-publication correction is part of scholarly quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate representation of reviewer comments and editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewer complained that the hoaxers 'selectively quoted from his review', turning an attempt to help into an indictment of the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting peer-review feedback selectively or out of context is misleading; ethical critique should use reviews and editorial communications honestly and transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific validity and ethical defensibility of sting operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple commentators concluded the experiment was 'flawed both experimentally and ethically, and failed to provide the evidence it sought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sting-style interventions intended as empirical claims must meet standards for experimental design, ethics (including deception and harm), and transparency if they are to justify broad claims about fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of motives and political framing in interpreting results
rubrics_metrics.description: The hoax 'received a polarized reception' and many responses debated whether the project was politically motivated or a legitimate expose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating critiques of scholarship, consider authors' motives and political framing, as they affect interpretation, credibility, and reception of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for peer reviewers' labor and editorial processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors expressed that referees 'put in a great deal of time and effort' and felt 'deeply disappointed' that fraudulent submissions wasted those efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical scholarly practice includes respect for the time and expertise of peer reviewers; actions that purposely waste reviewer labor are condemned by editors and academic communities.
